topics.title: Cells, microscopy and specialisation

cards.front: What does the cell membrane do, and what does the cell wall do?
cards.back: The cell membrane controls the substances entering and leaving the cell. The cell wall is a stiff cellulose layer outside the membrane that provides support.

cards.front: Name the three structures a plant cell has that an animal cell does not.
cards.back: Cellulose cell wall, large permanent vacuole, chloroplasts.

cards.front: What is the function of the large permanent vacuole?
cards.back: It contains cell sap and helps support the cell, so the cell keeps its shape.

cards.front: Give three ways a bacterial cell differs from a plant cell.
cards.back: No nucleus (its DNA is a loop free in the cytoplasm); the cell wall contains no cellulose; plasmids are present.

cards.front: Total magnification = ?
cards.back: eyepiece lens magnification × objective lens magnification. To find one lens, divide the total by the other — never subtract.

cards.front: The four steps for making a temporary slide.
cards.back: 1 Peel a thin piece of tissue. 2 Lay it flat on a slide. 3 Add a drop of iodine stain. 4 Lower a coverslip at an angle so no air bubbles are trapped.

cards.front: Cells of the same kind form a ____ ; these form an ____ ; and these form an ____ ____ .
cards.back: tissue; organ; organ system.

topics.title: Photosynthesis: equation and limiting factors

cards.front: Write the word equation for photosynthesis, including the two conditions.
cards.back: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, with light energy above the arrow and chlorophyll below it.

cards.front: Write the balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis. (Higher)
cards.back: $6CO_2 + 6H_2O \rightarrow C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2$

cards.front: What is a limiting factor?
cards.back: A factor that is below its optimum and so slows a process down. For photosynthesis the three are temperature, light intensity and carbon dioxide concentration.

cards.front: A rate-against-light-intensity graph is flat. What does that tell you?
cards.back: Light intensity is no longer the limiting factor — adding more light will not raise the rate. Something else, usually carbon dioxide concentration or temperature, is limiting now.

cards.front: Why is photosynthesis described as endothermic?
cards.back: Light energy is taken in from the surroundings and stored in the glucose.

cards.front: How do you answer 'describe the trend' on a graph, for both marks?
cards.back: Name both variables and the direction of change in one sentence, then quote values from the graph, including where it levels off.

cards.front: Why does the rate of photosynthesis fall above the optimum temperature?
cards.back: The enzymes are denatured: the shape of the active site changes irreversibly, so the substrate no longer fits.

cards.front: How do you calculate a percentage increase?
cards.back: change ÷ the original value × 100. The original value is the one you started from, never the new one.

cards.front: Equation: Photosynthesis
cards.back: carbon dioxide + water -> glucose + oxygen; 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2 (light, chlorophyll)

topics.title: Investigating photosynthesis (starch test, light, CO2, chlorophyll)

cards.front: The four steps of the starch test, with a reason for each.
cards.back: 1 Boil in water — kills the leaf and breaks the cells open. 2 Boil in ethanol with the Bunsen off — removes the chlorophyll. 3 Dip in hot water — softens the brittle leaf. 4 Add iodine solution on a white tile — blue-black means starch.

cards.front: How and why is a plant destarched?
cards.back: Leave it in the dark for 48 hours, so the starch already in the leaves is used up and any starch found afterwards must have been made during the investigation.

cards.front: What is the safety precaution when a leaf is heated in ethanol, and why?
cards.back: Turn the Bunsen burner off and stand the tube in hot water, because ethanol is flammable.

cards.front: Which solution absorbs carbon dioxide in a sealed flask, and which one releases it?
cards.back: Sodium hydroxide absorbs carbon dioxide. Sodium hydrogencarbonate releases it, which is how you give pondweed more.

cards.front: What does a variegated leaf show, and which parts turn blue-black?
cards.back: That chlorophyll is needed for photosynthesis. Only the green parts turn blue-black; the white parts have no chlorophyll and stay yellow-brown.

cards.front: What is the test for oxygen and its result?
cards.back: Put a glowing splint into the gas: it relights.

cards.front: Reliability or accuracy — which is improved by repeating a reading?
cards.back: Reliability. Repeats that agree show the result can be trusted. Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true value, and is improved by better technique or a better instrument.

topics.title: Leaf structure, gas exchange and compensation point

cards.front: Name the six layers of a mesophytic leaf from the top down.
cards.back: Waxy cuticle, upper epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll (with intercellular air spaces), lower epidermis, and the guard cells with their stomata.

cards.front: Give two adaptations of the palisade mesophyll and say what each is for.
cards.back: Many chloroplasts, to absorb the light; tightly packed end on just under the upper surface, so it receives the most light.

cards.front: Which layer of the leaf does most gas exchange take place in, and why?
cards.back: The spongy mesophyll: its cells are loosely arranged with large air spaces, giving a large surface area and letting gases diffuse through the leaf.

cards.front: Give three properties of the waxy cuticle.
cards.back: Transparent so light passes through; waterproof so water loss is reduced; a physical defence.

cards.front: Hydrogencarbonate indicator: high CO₂ ___ , normal CO₂ ___ , low CO₂ ___ .
cards.back: yellow; red; purple.

cards.front: A leaf in a sealed tube of indicator turns it yellow. What was happening?
cards.back: Only respiration: no photosynthesis, so carbon dioxide was released and its concentration rose.

cards.front: Define the compensation point.
cards.back: The light intensity at which photosynthesis and respiration are running at equal rates, so there is no net gas exchange.

cards.front: Why is a control tube with no leaf set up alongside the others?
cards.back: To show that any colour change in the other tubes was caused by the leaf and not by the light or the temperature.

cards.front: Does respiration stop in the light?
cards.back: No. A plant respires all the time. In bright light photosynthesis is simply faster, so the net exchange is carbon dioxide in and oxygen out.

cards.front: A plant is kept exactly at its compensation point for a week. Why does it not grow?
cards.back: Photosynthesis makes only as much glucose as respiration uses, so there is no surplus for growth or storage.

cards.front: Colour: Hydrogencarbonate indicator
cards.back: High CO2 yellow; normal CO2 red; low CO2 purple

topics.title: Food tests and reagent colour changes

cards.front: Benedict's solution: what does it test for, what colour does it start, what colour is a positive result, and what does it need?
cards.back: Reducing sugar. Blue at the start, brick red precipitate for a positive result, and it must be heated in a hot water bath.

cards.front: Iodine solution: substance, starting colour, positive colour.
cards.back: Starch. Yellow-brown at the start, blue-black for a positive result. No heating.

cards.front: Biuret: substance, starting colour, positive colour.
cards.back: Protein or amino acid. Blue at the start, lilac or purple for a positive result. No heating.

cards.front: How is the test for fat carried out, and what is the positive result?
cards.back: Shake the food with ethanol, then pour the liquid into a test tube of water. A white emulsion forms if fat is present.

cards.front: Which two food-test reagents both start off blue, and how do you tell their positive results apart?
cards.back: Benedict's and Biuret. Benedict's needs heating and ends brick red; Biuret needs no heating and ends lilac or purple.

cards.front: Test for Benedict's (reducing sugar, heat)
cards.back: Blue -> brick red precipitate

cards.front: Test for Iodine solution (starch)
cards.back: Yellow-brown -> blue-black

cards.front: Test for Biuret (protein)
cards.back: Blue -> lilac/purple

cards.front: Test for Ethanol (fat)
cards.back: Colourless -> white emulsion

topics.title: Biological molecules and the energy content of food

cards.front: What are carbohydrates, fats and proteins each made from?
cards.back: Carbohydrates: sugar units such as glucose. Fats and oils: fatty acids and glycerol. Proteins: amino acids.

cards.front: Storage or structural? starch ___, glycogen ___, cellulose ___, protein ___
cards.back: starch storage; glycogen storage; cellulose structural; protein structural (and functional).

cards.front: Name the two simple carbohydrates on this specification, and their use.
cards.back: Glucose and lactose, used as a source of energy and for storage.

cards.front: Write the two lines of working for the energy content of a food.
cards.back: energy transferred (J) = mass of water (g) × 4.2 × temperature rise (°C); energy per gram (J/g) = energy transferred ÷ mass of food burned (g).
keyWords: divide by the mass of food

cards.front: In the energy equation, which mass is used — the food or the water?
cards.back: The water. The water is what is being heated. The mass of food is used only in the second line, to find the energy per gram.

cards.front: Why is the measured energy content always too low, and what would improve it?
cards.back: Energy is lost to the air, the tube and the clamp, and some food does not burn completely. A draught shield, insulation or holding the food closer would make it more accurate. Repeating improves reliability, not accuracy.

topics.title: Enzymes, the lock and key model and digestion

cards.front: What is an enzyme?
cards.back: A protein molecule that acts as a biological catalyst: it speeds up the rate of a reaction without being used up.

cards.front: What is the active site, and what is a substrate?
cards.back: The active site is the part of the enzyme that the substrate fits into, because their shapes are complementary. The substrate is the molecule the enzyme acts on.

cards.front: What does substrate specificity mean?
cards.back: An enzyme catalyses only one type of substrate, because only that substrate has a shape complementary to its active site.

cards.front: carbohydrase (amylase) digests ___ into ___ ; protease digests ___ into ___ ; lipase digests ___ into ___ .
cards.back: starch into simple sugars; protein into amino acids; fat into fatty acids and glycerol.

cards.front: Why is digestion necessary?
cards.back: Food molecules are large and insoluble. Enzymes break them into small, soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the bloodstream.

cards.front: Give a commercial use of enzymes and say why it saves money.
cards.back: Biological washing powders contain protease and lipase, which remove protein and fat stains at 30-40 °C, so less energy is needed to heat the water.

cards.front: A molecule fits into the active site. Is it the substrate or the product?
cards.back: The substrate — it is what goes in. Products are what leave afterwards, and they no longer fit the active site.

cards.front: Enzyme
cards.back: A protein that acts as a biological catalyst, speeding up reactions without being used up.

topics.title: Temperature, pH, concentration and inhibitors on enzyme action

cards.front: What is the optimum for an enzyme?
cards.back: The value of a factor — temperature or pH — at which the reaction happens at its fastest rate.

cards.front: Define denaturation.
cards.back: An irreversible change in the shape of an enzyme, so that its active site is no longer complementary to the substrate and it cannot catalyse the reaction. Caused by high temperature or by pH away from the optimum.

cards.front: Why is an enzyme reaction slow at 5 °C? (Not 'the enzyme is denatured'.)
cards.back: The molecules have less energy and move more slowly, so there are fewer collisions between enzyme and substrate.

cards.front: Why does more enzyme give a faster reaction?
cards.back: There are more enzyme molecules, so more active sites are available and more substrate is being broken down at the same time.

cards.front: What is an inhibitor? (Higher)
cards.back: A molecule that fits into the active site of an enzyme but is not broken down, so it stops the substrate entering and reduces the rate.

cards.front: Give the method for Prescribed Practical B3 in five steps.
cards.back: 1 Iodine in the wells of a spotting tile. 2 Warm separate tubes of starch and amylase in the water bath. 3 Mix and start the stopwatch. 4 Every 30 s test a drop with iodine. 5 Record the time when it first stays yellow-brown, then repeat at other temperatures.

cards.front: A graph plots the TIME for a reaction against temperature. Where is the optimum?
cards.back: At the lowest point — the shortest time is the fastest reaction. On a rate graph it would be the highest point instead.

cards.front: How do you calculate a mean on a calculator without the BODMAS error?
cards.back: Put the addition in brackets: (A + B) ÷ 2. Then check the answer lies between A and B.

cards.front: Denaturation
cards.back: An irreversible change to the shape of the active site that inhibits enzyme action.

sections.title: 1.5 The Respiratory System, Breathing and Respiration

topics.title: Respiratory surfaces and the effect of exercise on breathing

cards.front: List the six adaptations of a respiratory surface.
cards.back: Large surface area, thin, moist, permeable, good blood supply, and the diffusion gradient maintained.

cards.front: Thin means a short ____ ____ ; moist means gases can ____ ; a good blood supply maintains the ____ ____ .
cards.back: diffusion distance; dissolve; diffusion gradient.

cards.front: At an alveolus, which way does oxygen diffuse and which way does carbon dioxide diffuse?
cards.back: Oxygen diffuses out of the alveolus into the blood; carbon dioxide diffuses out of the blood into the alveolus. Each gas moves from where it is more concentrated to where it is less.

cards.front: What two things happen to breathing during exercise, and why?
cards.back: The rate and the depth of breathing both increase, because the muscles respire faster and so need more oxygen and produce more carbon dioxide to remove.

cards.front: How do you give 'evidence from a graph' so it scores?
cards.back: Name both things being compared, quote a value for each, and say which is higher or lower. A sentence with no number is not evidence.

topics.title: Aerobic respiration and its equation

cards.front: Write the word equation for aerobic respiration.
cards.back: glucose + oxygen → energy + carbon dioxide + water

cards.front: Write the balanced symbol equation for aerobic respiration. (Higher)
cards.back: $C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \rightarrow \text{energy} + 6CO_2 + 6H_2O$

cards.front: In which equation does 'energy' go on the arrow, and in which is it written as a product?
cards.back: On the arrow in photosynthesis, which is endothermic and needs light supplied. As a product in respiration, which is exothermic and gives energy out.

cards.front: Name the five uses of the energy released by respiration.
cards.back: Heat, movement, growth, reproduction, and active uptake or transport.

cards.front: Where and how often does respiration happen?
cards.back: In the mitochondria, in every living cell, continuously — day and night, in plants as well as animals.

cards.front: What is the difference between breathing and respiration?
cards.back: Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs. Respiration is a chemical reaction inside cells, in the mitochondria, that releases energy from glucose.

cards.front: A flask of germinating peas warms up but a flask of boiled peas does not. What does that show, and what is the second flask for?
cards.back: Respiration is exothermic — it releases energy as heat. The boiled peas are the control, showing the rise was caused by the living peas and not by the surroundings.

cards.front: Why does active transport need respiration?
cards.back: Active transport moves substances against the concentration gradient, which needs energy, and that energy is released by respiration.

cards.front: Equation: Aerobic respiration
cards.back: glucose + oxygen -> energy + carbon dioxide + water; C6H12O6 + 6O2 -> energy + 6CO2 + 6H2O

topics.title: Anaerobic respiration in muscle and yeast

cards.front: For a mammalian muscle, write the word equation for anaerobic respiration.
cards.back: glucose → energy + lactic acid

cards.front: Write the word equation for anaerobic respiration in yeast.
cards.back: glucose → energy + alcohol + carbon dioxide

cards.front: Which anaerobic product belongs to muscle and which to yeast?
cards.back: Lactic acid is muscle. Alcohol and carbon dioxide are yeast. Muscle produces no gas at all.

cards.front: Give one similarity and one difference between aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
cards.back: Both use glucose and release energy. Aerobic needs oxygen and releases much more energy per glucose; anaerobic needs none and releases much less.

cards.front: How do you show that yeast is respiring, and what is the oil for?
cards.back: Bubble the gas through limewater: it turns milky, showing carbon dioxide. The oil layer keeps air out so the respiration is anaerobic.

cards.front: Equation: Anaerobic respiration (muscle)
cards.back: glucose -> energy + lactic acid

cards.front: Equation: Anaerobic respiration (yeast)
cards.back: glucose -> energy + alcohol + carbon dioxide

topics.title: Nervous and hormonal communication, CNS, voluntary and reflex actions

cards.front: Name the two organs of the central nervous system and say what it does.
cards.back: The brain and the spinal cord. It controls and co-ordinates the responses between receptors and effectors.

cards.front: stimulus → ____ → ____ → ____ → response
cards.back: receptor → central nervous system → effector.

cards.front: What is an effector, and what is it never?
cards.back: A muscle or a gland — the thing that carries out the response. It is never the stimulus, a nerve, or the body part that moves.

cards.front: Give three differences between the nervous and hormonal systems.
cards.back: Nervous: electrical impulses along neurones, fast, short-lived. Hormonal: chemical hormones in the blood, slower, longer-lasting.

cards.front: How do voluntary and reflex actions differ?
cards.back: A voluntary action is under conscious control and is slower; a reflex action is automatic, not consciously controlled, and much faster.

topics.title: The spinal reflex arc

cards.front: Write the pathway of a spinal reflex arc, from stimulus to response.
cards.back: stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → (synapse) → association neurone → (synapse) → motor neurone → effector → response.

cards.front: What is a synapse, and how does an impulse cross it?
cards.back: The gap between two neurones. A chemical is released, diffuses across the gap and starts a new impulse in the next neurone.

cards.front: How many synapses are there in a spinal reflex arc, and where?
cards.back: Two: one between the sensory and association neurones, and one between the association and motor neurones.

cards.front: Why does a pathway with more synapses give a slower response?
cards.back: At each synapse a chemical has to be released and diffuse across the gap, which is slower than conduction along a neurone, so every extra gap adds a delay.

cards.front: Which word does CCEA use for the middle neurone of the reflex arc?
cards.back: Association neurone. 'Relay neurone' is the same cell, but the specification and the mark schemes say association.

cards.front: Which structure co-ordinates a spinal reflex, and why does that make it fast?
cards.back: The spinal cord. The impulse does not have to travel to the brain and no conscious decision is made, so the pathway is short and the response is quick.

cards.front: What does a receptor do, in the specification's words?
cards.back: It detects stimuli in the environment and produces nerve impulses.

topics.title: Homeostasis, insulin and diabetes

cards.front: What is homeostasis, and which two examples does this specification use?
cards.back: Maintaining a constant internal environment so that cells and enzymes function properly. The two examples are controlling blood glucose concentration and osmoregulation.

cards.front: Describe the loop that lowers blood glucose, in five steps.
cards.back: 1 The pancreas monitors blood glucose. 2 It rises after a meal. 3 The pancreas releases insulin into the blood. 4 Insulin makes the liver absorb glucose. 5 Liver cells respire it or store it as glycogen.

cards.front: What is a hormone?
cards.back: A chemical messenger produced by a gland and released into the blood, which carries it to a target organ where it acts.

cards.front: Give two ways insulin lowers blood glucose — without repeating the question.
cards.back: It makes the liver absorb glucose from the blood, and the liver cells respire it or convert it to glycogen and store it.

cards.front: Type 1: the pancreas ____ producing insulin, usually ____ in life. Type 2: the pancreas ____ produces less insulin, linked to ____ .
cards.back: stops; early; gradually; lifestyle factors and obesity.

cards.front: Name the four symptoms of diabetes and four possible long-term effects.
cards.back: Symptoms: high blood glucose, glucose in the urine, lethargy, thirst. Long-term effects: eye damage, kidney failure, heart disease, strokes.

cards.front: Why is the number of people with diabetes rising, and what makes that hard to judge?
cards.back: More obesity, diets higher in sugar and less physical activity all raise Type 2 diabetes. But better diagnosis also means more of the people who already had it are counted, so part of the rise is better detection.

cards.front: Homeostasis
cards.back: Maintaining a constant internal environment for the proper functioning of cells and enzymes.

cards.front: Hormone
cards.back: A chemical messenger produced by a gland and released into the blood, which carries it to a target organ.

topics.title: The excretory system, osmoregulation and ADH

cards.front: Name the parts of the excretory system, following the urine from where it is made to where it leaves.
cards.back: Kidney (which makes it), ureter (which carries it to the bladder), bladder (which stores it), urethra (which carries it out). Blood arrives by the renal artery and leaves by the renal vein.

cards.front: Which organ produces urine, and which one only stores it?
cards.back: The kidney produces urine; the bladder stores it.

cards.front: The three regions of the kidney named by the specification are the ____ (outer), the ____ (inner) and the ____ , where urine collects.
cards.back: cortex; medulla; pelvis.

cards.front: Give the three ways water is gained and the three ways it is lost.
cards.back: Gained: in food, in drink, and made by respiration. Lost: evaporation of sweat, evaporation during breathing, and urine produced by the kidney.

cards.front: What is the kidney's homeostatic role?
cards.back: It filters the blood and controls how much water is reabsorbed, so the volume of urine changes to keep the body's water content constant.

cards.front: More ADH — what happens to water reabsorption, urine volume and urine concentration? (Higher)
cards.back: More water is reabsorbed, a smaller volume of urine is produced, and the urine is more concentrated.

cards.front: What does ADH stand for, and what is its target organ?
cards.back: Antidiuretic hormone. Its target organ is the kidney, and it reaches it in the blood.

topics.title: Plant hormones and phototropism

cards.front: What is phototropism?
cards.back: The growth of a stem towards light: differential growth of cells caused by an uneven distribution of auxin in response to light coming from one direction.

cards.front: Name the plant hormone that causes phototropism.
cards.back: Auxin.

cards.front: Give the four stages of phototropism in order (Higher).
cards.back: Auxin is produced at the tip of the shoot; it moves down the shoot; light causes an uneven distribution, with more auxin on the shaded side; auxin causes cell elongation, so the shaded side grows longer and the shoot bends towards the light.

cards.front: Which side of a shoot has more auxin, and why does that make it bend towards the light?
cards.back: The shaded side. Auxin makes cells elongate, so the shaded side grows longer than the lit side, and a stem that is longer on one side curves towards the other — towards the light.

cards.front: Does auxin make cells divide or make them longer?
cards.back: Longer. Auxin causes cell elongation. Writing 'more cells' or 'the cells divide' describes cell division and does not earn the elongation mark.

cards.front: A shoot has its tip cut off and is then lit from one side. What two things happen?
cards.back: It does not bend and it does not grow, because the tip is where the auxin is produced.

cards.front: Why is 'the shoot moves towards the light' not enough for the mark?
cards.back: A tropism is growth, not movement, and the mark scheme wants a direction. Write that the shoot bends or grows towards the light.

cards.front: How do you calculate a percentage increase?
cards.back: Increase divided by the ORIGINAL value, multiplied by 100. Dividing by the final value is the error examiners report most often on these questions.

topics.title: Ecological terms, fieldwork and quadrat sampling

cards.front: Define population, community and ecosystem.
cards.back: A population is all the organisms of one species in a habitat. A community is all the populations of all the species in that habitat. An ecosystem is the community together with the non-living surroundings it interacts with.

cards.front: What is biodiversity?
cards.back: The number of different species of plants and animals present.

cards.front: Name the five abiotic factors the specification lists, and one instrument for each.
cards.back: Wind speed (anemometer), water content (balance, by drying and reweighing), pH (pH meter), light (light meter) and temperature (thermometer).

cards.front: How do you place a quadrat at random?
cards.back: Lay two tape measures along two edges at right angles, generate pairs of random numbers and use each pair as a co-ordinate for one quadrat position.

cards.front: When do you use a belt transect rather than random sampling?
cards.back: When you want to know how a species changes across a habitat — from a path to a hedge, or up a beach. A transect is not random sampling.

cards.front: Which two things do examiners say go missing from the six-mark fieldwork answer?
cards.back: The name of the apparatus — the quadrat — and the use of a key to identify the species. Write both in your first two sentences.

cards.front: How do you scale a mean quadrat count up to a whole field?
cards.back: Multiply the mean number per quadrat by the area of the field divided by the area of the quadrat.

cards.front: Does repeating a quadrat count improve reliability or accuracy?
cards.back: Reliability. Repeats allow a mean and show up an anomalous result. Accuracy is how close a single measurement is to the true value, and depends on how carefully you count.

cards.front: Ecosystem terms
cards.back: Biodiversity, population, habitat, environment, community, ecosystem - CCEA Biology Glossary of Terms wording.

topics.title: Adaptation, competition, producers and food webs

cards.front: What is the source of energy for most ecosystems, and what captures it?
cards.back: The Sun. Green plants — the producers — capture it by photosynthesis and make it available to consumers.

cards.front: What does an arrow in a food chain represent?
cards.back: Consumption, and the transfer of energy and substances such as carbon and nitrogen. It runs from the organism that is eaten to the organism that eats it.

cards.front: What do plants compete for, and what do animals compete for?
cards.back: Plants: water, light, space, minerals. Animals: water, food, territory, mates, and they must avoid predators. Plants never compete for food.

cards.front: Two species decline when a third arrives, but none of them eats the others. What is the relationship called?
cards.back: Competition — they need the same limited resource. Calling a competitor a predator is the error examiners report on the squirrel question.

cards.front: Which trophic level holds the producers, and what can never be at that level?
cards.back: Level 1 holds the producers, which are green plants. No animal can be at Level 1.

topics.title: Decomposition and the carbon cycle

cards.front: Describe how a saprophytic fungus feeds, in three steps.
cards.back: It secretes enzymes out of its cells onto the dead material; the enzymes digest it outside the cells (extracellular digestion); the small soluble products are absorbed.

cards.front: What is a saprophyte, and what does it form in the soil?
cards.back: An organism that feeds on dead material. Saprophytic fungi and bacteria recycle nutrients and form humus.

cards.front: Which three conditions make decay fastest?
cards.back: Warm, moist and aerobic (plenty of oxygen).

cards.front: Which processes ADD carbon dioxide to the air, and which REMOVES it?
cards.back: Adds: respiration, combustion, decomposition. Removes: photosynthesis, and nothing else. Respiration never goes in the removing column.

cards.front: Name the eight processes the specification lists in the carbon cycle.
cards.back: Photosynthesis, respiration, combustion, fossilisation, feeding, excretion, egestion and decomposition.

cards.front: Why does a plant take carbon dioxide in during the day but give it out at night?
cards.back: It photosynthesises and respires all the time. In the light photosynthesis is faster, so carbon dioxide moves in overall; in the dark photosynthesis stops and only respiration continues, so carbon dioxide moves out.

cards.front: How do you calculate a rate of decomposition in grams per week?
cards.back: Subtract the final mass from the starting mass, then divide by the total number of weeks the experiment ran — not by the gap between readings.

cards.front: Why is decay very slow in a waterlogged soil or a sealed bag?
cards.back: There is almost no oxygen, so the decomposers cannot respire aerobically; they release much less energy, grow slowly and break material down slowly.

topics.title: The nitrogen cycle

cards.front: Name the four processes of the nitrogen cycle.
cards.back: nitrogen fixation, decomposition, nitrification, denitrification.

cards.front: Name the four types of bacteria, one for each process.
cards.back: Nitrogen-fixing, decomposing (saprophytic), nitrifying and denitrifying bacteria.

cards.front: What does nitrogen fixation change, and into what?
cards.back: Nitrogen gas from the air into nitrates, which plants can absorb. It is done by nitrogen-fixing bacteria in the soil and in root nodules, and by lightning. (Lightning is background only: this specification asks for the bacteria.)

cards.front: What does decomposition change, and into what?
cards.back: Protein in dead material and urea in waste into ammonium compounds, by decomposing (saprophytic) bacteria and fungi.

cards.front: What does nitrification change, and into what?
cards.back: Ammonium compounds into nitrites and then into nitrates, by nitrifying bacteria. They are aerobic. (Not on this specification: the nitrite step — CCEA asks only for ammonium compounds → nitrates.)

cards.front: What does denitrification change, and into what?
cards.back: Nitrates back into nitrogen gas, by denitrifying bacteria. They are anaerobic.

cards.front: Explain, as a chain, why a waterlogged soil loses nitrate.
cards.back: The air spaces fill with water, so there is no oxygen; denitrifying bacteria are anaerobic so they multiply and convert nitrate into nitrogen gas; the aerobic nitrifying and nitrogen-fixing bacteria become less active, so less nitrate is made; so there is less nitrate for plants.

cards.front: What do plants use nitrate for, and how do animals get their nitrogen?
cards.back: Plants absorb nitrate through their roots and use it to make amino acids and then proteins. Animals get nitrogen by eating plants or other animals and digesting their protein.

cards.front: A question asks for the TYPE OF BACTERIA. What must your answer end in?
cards.back: -ing: nitrogen-fixing, nitrifying, denitrifying, decomposing. Processes end in -ation or -ition, and giving a process where bacteria were asked for earns nothing.

cards.front: Why does a farmer sow clover in a field for a season?
cards.back: Clover is a legume with root nodules containing nitrogen-fixing bacteria, which convert nitrogen gas into nitrate and raise the soil's nitrate content for the next crop.

topics.title: Mineral uptake by roots and eutrophication

cards.front: What adapts a root hair cell for absorption, and what is CCEA's word for that feature?
cards.back: It has an extension — a long narrow projection — which gives it a large surface area. Describe it as an extension, not as a hair like one on your head.

cards.front: Give the four things you must say about active transport.
cards.back: It moves mineral ions; against the concentration gradient, from low to high; it requires energy; and the energy comes from respiration.

cards.front: How does water enter a root hair cell, and does it need energy?
cards.back: By osmosis, down its own gradient. It needs no energy at all. Saying water enters by active transport is an error examiners have reported in two series.

cards.front: Which mineral do plants absorb to make proteins?
cards.back: Nitrate. (Magnesium is not on this specification.)

cards.front: Why does nitrate uptake almost stop when there is no oxygen around a root?
cards.back: Active transport needs energy, and that energy comes from aerobic respiration. With no oxygen there is no aerobic respiration, so little energy and almost no uptake.

cards.front: Give the seven stages of eutrophication in order.
cards.back: 1 fertiliser or sewage washed in; 2 algae and plants grow rapidly; 3 shading, and nitrate runs out; 4 plants and algae die; 5 aerobic bacteria decompose them; 6 oxygen used up; 7 fish and invertebrates die

cards.front: What actually uses up the oxygen in eutrophication?
cards.back: Aerobic decomposing bacteria, respiring as they feed on the dead algae and plants. Living algae photosynthesise and add oxygen.

cards.front: Why does 'nutrients are washed into the river' score nothing?
cards.back: The mark is for naming the ion: nitrate (or phosphate). Summer 2024 examiners reported that 'nutrients' earned nothing for that point.

cards.front: Why do the water plants on a lake bed die during eutrophication?
cards.back: The algal bloom at the surface shades them so they cannot photosynthesise, and the nitrate has been used up.

cards.front: Why do fish die at the end of the eutrophication sequence?
cards.back: There is too little dissolved oxygen left in the water for them to respire.

cards.front: Active transport
cards.back: Movement of substances against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration (Higher).
